lead: On the grid the inverter does not set the voltage: the grid does. A grid-tied inverter instead injects a controlled sine current in step with the grid voltage. A phase-locked loop (PLL) finds the grid angle, an outer loop sets how much current is needed, and a fast inner current loop switches the bridge so that the measured current follows the reference. Rooftop solar, battery storage and wind converters work this way, and the same loops set the power factor, keep the harmonics low and disconnect the inverter if the grid fails.
prereq: You need: sinusoidal PWM and phasors with real and reactive power.

sections.h3: The grid sets the voltage, the inverter sets the current

blocks.text: The grid is a stiff voltage source: its amplitude and frequency barely move when one inverter connects. Two voltage sources joined by a small inductance would exchange a current set only by their small difference, which is hard to control. So the inverter behaves as a controlled current source behind its filter inductance.

blocks.where: i* is the current reference in amperes, I* its peak, θ the grid angle from the PLL and φ* the commanded phase shift (0 for unity power factor).

blocks.text: Single-phase power is P = V I cos φ and Q = V I sin φ, with V and I rms values and φ the angle between them; in three-phase, P = √3 V<sub>L</sub> I cos φ with V<sub>L</sub> the line voltage. At fixed I*, changing φ* trades real power for reactive power, so the outer loop must set I* and φ* together.

items: Measure the grid voltage; the PLL gives θ and the frequency.

The DC-link voltage loop compares the link voltage with its set value: if power arrives faster than it leaves, the voltage rises and I* is raised. (A solar maximum power point tracker sets the link voltage set-point; it does not set I* directly.)
Form i* from θ, I* and φ*.
The current controller compares the measured i with i* and drives the bridge.
An L or LCL filter removes the switching ripple before the grid.

sections.h3: Current controllers and the LCL filter

blocks.text: The current loop must be much faster than the DC-link loop: a link loop of 10 to 20 Hz bandwidth, a current loop of 1 to 2 kHz bandwidth, with the bridge switching and sampling at 10 to 20 kHz.

Hysteresis control switches the bridge whenever the current leaves a band of width h around i*. It is simple and very fast, but its switching frequency changes with the grid voltage and the inductance, which makes the filter hard to design. In the synchronous (dq) frame, the PLL angle turns the three-phase currents into two DC quantities, i<sub>d</sub> (active) and i<sub>q</sub> (reactive); PI controllers then give zero steady-state error, with ωL cross-coupling terms cancelled. A proportional-resonant (PR) controller, K<sub>p</sub> + K<sub>r</sub> s/(s² + ω<sub>0</sub>²), does the same in the stationary frame by having very high gain at the grid frequency ω<sub>0</sub>.
fres = (1/2π)√((L1 + L2)/(L1 L2 C)) L1 is the inverter-side inductance, L2 the grid-side inductance and C the filter capacitance; fres in hertz.

An LCL filter attenuates the switching ripple at 60 dB per decade, far better than a single L, with less inductance. Its resonance must be damped, by a resistor in series with C or by active damping in the controller, and is usually placed between ten times the grid frequency and half the switching frequency.

sections.h3: Islanding, power factor and off-grid operation

blocks.text: If the grid is disconnected for repair, an inverter that kept feeding local loads would energise the line and endanger the line crew. Anti-islanding protection trips it: passive methods watch for voltage or frequency moving out of limits, and active methods inject a small disturbance and watch the response. Grid codes set the time within which the inverter must stop.

An off-grid (stand-alone) inverter has no grid to follow, so it controls its own voltage amplitude and frequency, often with droop so that several units share the load. Hybrid inverters change between the two modes when the grid fails.

examples.question: A rooftop solar inverter sends P = 5 kW into a 230 V, 50 Hz single-phase grid. (a) Find the rms and peak current reference at unity power factor. (b) The grid rises to 240 V; find the new current and the power a frozen reference would give. (c) At 230 V the operator asks for power factor 0.9 with the same 5 kW; find the current, the reactive power and φ*.
steps: (b) I = 5000/240 = 20.83 A rms. A reference frozen at 21.74 A would give 240 × 21.74 = 5217 W, so the DC-link loop must lower I*.
examples.answer: (a) 21.74 A rms, 30.74 A peak; (b) 20.83 A, against 5217 W if frozen; (c) 24.15 A, Q = 2422 var, φ* = 25.8°.

examples.question: The same 5 kW inverter has an LCL filter with L<sub>1</sub> = 2 mH, L<sub>2</sub> = 1 mH and C = 10 μF, and a 400 V DC link with unipolar SPWM. Find the filter resonance, the inverter voltage needed at unity power factor, and the modulation index.
steps: f<sub>res</sub> = (1/2π)√((2 + 1) × 10⁻³/(2 × 10⁻³ × 1 × 10⁻³ × 10 × 10⁻⁶)) = (1/2π)√(1.5 × 10⁸) = (1/2π) × 12247 = 1949 Hz, well above 500 Hz and below half of a 10 kHz switching frequency.
At 50 Hz the capacitor current is small, so treat the filter as L<sub>1</sub> + L<sub>2</sub> = 3 mH: X = 2π × 50 × 0.003 = 0.9425 Ω.
The current is in phase with the grid voltage, so V<sub>inv</sub> = V<sub>g</sub> + jXI = 230 + j(0.9425 × 21.74) = 230 + j20.49 V.
|V<sub>inv</sub>| = √(230² + 20.49²) = 230.91 V rms, leading the grid by δ = tan⁻¹(20.49/230) = 5.09°.
examples.answer: f<sub>res</sub> = 1949 Hz; V<sub>inv</sub> = 230.91 V rms leading by 5.09°; m<sub>a</sub> = 0.816.

traps: A grid-tied inverter commands current, not voltage; its voltage is whatever the grid plus the filter drop needs.
The sine table uses the peak I*, cable and meter ratings use the rms; do not mix them.
In three-phase use P = √3 V<sub>L</sub> I cos φ with the line voltage; using the phase voltage gives a current √3 times too large.
An LCL filter is not just a big L: undamped, its resonance can make the current loop oscillate.
Anti-islanding means the inverter must stop when the grid is lost; an off-grid inverter is designed to run alone.

quiz.q: What does the PLL give the current controller?
quiz.a: The grid angle θ (and frequency), so the current reference is in step with the grid voltage.

quiz.q: Why is a grid-tied inverter controlled as a current source?
quiz.a: The grid already fixes the voltage; between two voltage sources the current is set by a small difference across a small impedance and is hard to control, so the inverter commands the current directly.

quiz.q: A 10 kW single-phase inverter feeds a 230 V grid at unity power factor. Find the rms and peak current.
A three-phase 10 kW inverter feeds a 400 V line-to-line grid at unity power factor. Find the line current.
Compare hysteresis and dq PI current control.
quiz.a: Hysteresis: simple, fastest response, but variable switching frequency and a harder filter design. dq PI: fixed switching frequency and zero steady-state error, but needs the PLL angle, frame transforms and decoupling terms.

quiz.q: At a fixed current amplitude, the operator changes φ* from 0 to 25.8°. What happens to P and Q?
quiz.a: P = VI cos φ falls to 90 % and Q = VI sin φ rises from zero to 44 % of VI; to keep P constant the amplitude must rise by 1/0.9.

beyond: Not for the exam. Grid-forming inverters set their own voltage and frequency like a synchronous machine, so that grids with little rotating inertia stay stable. Search for grid-forming inverters, virtual synchronous machines and LCL active damping.
